# **Anti-statist sustainability backlash: Libertarianism and the erosion of state capacities in Argentina under Javier Milei**

# **1\. Introduction**

In recent years, sustainability has faced growing political backlash across multiple regions of the world. Climate policy in particular has become increasingly contested amid rising polarization, economic insecurity, geopolitical tensions, and broader crises of democratic legitimacy (references). These backlash dynamics take different forms depending on national political contexts. In some cases, opposition centers on climate skepticism and fossil-fuel interests; in others, sustainability policy is criticized as economically harmful, socially exclusionary, technocratic, or associated with globalist political agendas. More recently, far-right and anti-establishment movements in several countries have increasingly framed environmental regulation, climate governance, and sustainability transitions as threats to national sovereignty, economic freedom, or traditional social orders (references).

Argentina under President Javier Milei represents a particularly distinctive case within these broader dynamics. Milei came to power in December 2023 amid severe economic crisis, triple-digit inflation, institutional distrust, and widespread disillusionment with the traditional political establishment. Presenting himself as an anti-system outsider committed to a radical rupture with what he termed “*la casta”* (the caste), Milei advanced a political project combining radical market liberalism with an antagonistic and highly personalized political style. Described as a form of “libertarian populism” (Merke, 2026\) his discourse portrays the state not as a legitimate mechanism for collective coordination or long-term planning, but as an inherently coercive, inefficient, and predatory actor. Shortly after taking office, his government launched a broad agenda of deregulation, fiscal austerity, institutional restructuring, and public-spending reduction aimed at radically shrinking the role of the state in economic and social life.

This libertarian orientation has important implications for sustainability governance. Sustainability transitions depend heavily on long-term public coordination, regulatory institutions, scientific expertise, planning capacities, and international cooperation (References). Yet Milei’s discourse frequently questions the legitimacy not only of state intervention, but also of the epistemic foundations underpinning sustainability governance itself. Climate science, environmental regulation, and multilateral sustainability agendas are often reframed as ideological or bureaucratic instruments that constrain individual freedom and market dynamics. More broadly, institutions and expert bodies are increasingly portrayed not as legitimate sites of mediation and coordination, but as obstacles to be bypassed or dismantled (Merke, 2026). In this context, public scientific institutions become politically vulnerable because they provide knowledge infrastructures and legitimacy for regulatory intervention and collective action.

Building on literature on climate-policy backlash, policy dismantling, and state capacity, this article examines how libertarian narratives reshape sustainability policy and the public scientific capacities underpinning climate and environmental governance in Argentina. We conceptualize sustainability governance in the context of Milei government as a distinctive form of “anti-statist sustainability backlash”: rather than merely opposing specific environmental regulations, this backlash targets the institutional, regulatory, and epistemic infrastructures required for sustainability transitions. The article asks: How does libertarian discourse justify the dismantling of sustainability policy, and how does this affect state capabilities for governing sustainability transitions in Argentina?

To address this question, we analyze the Argentine case from two complementary perspectives. First, we conduct a narrative analysis of the president’s public discourses official justifications and public communications to identify how state intervention, sustainability policy, climate governance, and scientific expertise are problematized and reframed. Second, we trace changes in state capabilities by examining institutional reorganizations, budget reallocation and policy changes affecting the implementation of sustainability policy and support for public science. Empirically, the article relies on document analysis of presidential speeches, executive decrees, governmental restructuring processes, and key policy decisions in the fields of energy, environment, and science policy.

We argue that libertarian governance can generate sustainability-policy retrenchment through a dual mechanism: discursive delegitimization of regulation and expertise, coupled with capability erosion that weakens the state’s ability to design, finance, coordinate, and enforce sustainability policy \-even when formal climate commitments remain in place. In doing so, the article contributes to emerging debates on sustainability-policy backlash by showing how libertarian ideas may operationalize policy dismantling through state transformation and institutional hollowing-out rather than primarily through overt authoritarian closure.

# **2\. Theoretical Background**

## 2.1 Climate obstructionism and sustainability-policy backlash

Political opposition to climate and sustainability policies has attracted growing scholarly attention over the past two decades. Early research focused primarily on climate denial, examining how fossil-fuel interests, conservative think tanks, contrarian scientists, and sympathetic media organizations sought to challenge the scientific consensus on anthropogenic climate change and resist regulatory intervention (McCright & Dunlap, 2000; Jacques, Dunlap, & Freeman, 2008; Oreskes & Conway, 2010; Brulle, 2014). Rather than simply producing alternative scientific claims, these actors worked to maintain political uncertainty long after scientific consensus had emerged, thereby delaying regulatory responses and preserving existing economic interests (Dunlap & McCright, 2015; Brulle, 2021).

As the scientific consensus became increasingly difficult to contest, however, political opposition evolved beyond explicit denial. Instead of rejecting climate science outright, many actors shifted their attention towards questioning the urgency, effectiveness, fairness, or economic desirability of climate policies. Lamb et al. (2020) conceptualize these narratives as discourses of climate delay, identifying a range of rhetorical strategies that acknowledge climate change while discouraging transformative action. These include emphasizing the economic costs of mitigation, promoting incremental or insufficient technological solutions, shifting responsibility onto other actors or countries, and portraying ambitious climate action as unrealistic or socially unacceptable. Climate obstruction therefore increasingly operates through the contestation of policy responses rather than the rejection of climate science itself (Lamb et al., 2020; Stoddard et al., 2021).

More recently, scholars have argued that obstructionopposition extends beyond individual climate policies to encompass broader resistance to sustainability transitions. Research on climate backlash, green backlash, anti-environmental countermovements, and resistance to net-zero transitions emphasizes that sustainability policies have become embedded within wider political conflicts over economic redistribution, state intervention, cultural identity, national sovereignty, and the authority of scientific expertise (Lockwood, 2018; Forchtner, 2019; Colgan, Green, & Hale, 2021; Bosetti, 2026). Rather than opposing only specific environmental measures, political actors increasingly challenge the broader societal transformations associated with decarbonization, environmental protection, and sustainability governance. As Bosetti (2026) argues, contemporary green backlash should be understood as a multidimensional political phenomenon in which environmental policies become symbolic targets within wider ideological conflicts over the role of the state, markets, expertise, and social change.

This broader perspective has also expanded the understanding of climate obstruction. Rather than referring solely to organized climate denial, obstruction is increasingly conceptualized as a repertoire of discursive and institutional practices aimed at delaying, weakening, or delegitimizing climate and sustainability governance (Brulle, 2021; Stoddard et al., 2021). These practices may include attacks on scientific expertise, regulatory rollback, reductions in environmental funding, administrative weakening, or the framing of sustainability policies as economically harmful, ideologically motivated, or democratically illegitimate. Climate obstruction thus concerns not only whether governments adopt environmental policies, but also whether they sustain the institutional conditions necessary for their implementation.

Despite these important advances, three limitations remain. First, much of the literature continues to focus on climate policy rather than the broader governance structures underpinning sustainability transitions. Second, empirical attention has concentrated primarily on right-wing populist or conservative opposition rooted in distributive conflicts, sectoral interests, or nationalist politics, particularly in Europe and North America (Lockwood, 2018; Forchtner, 2019). Comparatively less attention has been devoted to cases from the Global South and to political projects whose primary objective is not merely to oppose environmental regulation but to fundamentally redefine the role of the state. Finally, while obstruction and backlash research has documented how political actors contest the legitimacy of sustainability policies, it has devoted comparatively little attention to how these narratives translate into the weakening of the institutional and organizational capacities required for sustainability governance.

These limitations are particularly relevant for understanding the Argentine case under Javier Milei. Rather than opposing only particular environmental or climate policies, the Milei administration appears to articulate a broader critique of public intervention, scientific expertise, and state coordination. To understand this distinctive configuration, it is therefore necessary to complement the obstruction and backlash literature with scholarship on libertarian populism, anti-statist governance, policy dismantling, and state capacity.

## 2.2 Libertarian populism and anti-statist governance

Although the literature on climate obstruction and sustainability-policy backlash explains why climate and environmental policies become politically contested, it provides only a partial explanation for the Argentine case. Under the Milei administration, environmental policy is challenged as part of a broader project of state retrenchment rather than as an isolated policy domain. Understanding this distinctive configuration therefore requires engaging with scholarship on populism, libertarianism, and anti-statist governance.

Research on right-wing populism has consistently shown that environmental and climate policies are frequently framed as products of detached political elites, technocratic governance, and international organizations that undermine national sovereignty and individual freedoms (Mudde, 2007; Müller, 2016; Lockwood, 2018; Forchtner, 2019; Norris & Inglehart, 2019). Climate policy thus becomes embedded within broader conflicts over representation, expertise, and the legitimacy of liberal democratic institutions. In Europe and North America, opposition to environmental regulation has often combined anti-elitism, distrust of scientific expertise, nationalism, and resistance to supranational governance (Forchtner & Kølvraa, 2015; Kulin et al., 2021; Küppers, 2022). Similar dynamics have increasingly been identified in the Global South, where environmental governance has become intertwined with debates over sovereignty, development, and resource nationalism. The Bolsonaro administration in Brazil, for example, combined environmental deregulation with attacks on environmental agencies, scientific institutions, and international environmental governance, while justifying these reforms through narratives of national development, territorial sovereignty, and resistance to foreign interference (Hochstetler, 2021; Pereira & Viola, 2022; Viola & Gonçalves, 2022).

The Argentine case shares several characteristics with these broader populist dynamics, including anti-elitism, criticism of international organizations, and skepticism towards environmental regulation. However, the ideological foundations of the Milei administration differ in important respects. Rather than primarily advancing a nationalist or productivist agenda, Milei explicitly presents his government as the world's first genuinely libertarian administration (Merke, 2026). While libertarian ideas have long circulated in economic and political thought, they have rarely been implemented as an explicit governing programme at the national level, and empirical scholarship on libertarian governments is correspondingly scarce. The libertarian intellectual tradition has nonethelessWhile empirical studies of libertarian governments remain scarce, the libertarian intellectual tradition has long emphasized individual liberty, market coordination, limited government, and skepticism toward state intervention. Hayek's critique of central planning argued that knowledge is inherently dispersed throughout society and that governments cannot effectively coordinate economic activity through centralized decision-making (Hayek, 1945, 1960). Later neoliberal scholarship similarly challenged the expansion of state regulation and highlighted the coordinating role of competitive markets (Harvey, 2005; Mirowski, 2013; Plehwe, 2014). Although these traditions do not reject scientific knowledge per se, they question the capacity and legitimacy of governments to organize society through planning, regulation, and expert administration. The knowledge problem does not require disputing the validity of expert knowledge; it holds that such knowledge, however sound, cannot be centrally aggregated and acted upon. Opposition to expert-guided governance can therefore be articulated without contesting expertise itself, targeting instead the state's competence and legitimacy to translate knowledge into collective action. Subsequent scholarship has documented how this argument was propagated beyond academic economics through a transnational network of think tanks, foundations, and intellectual entrepreneurs that translated it into a programmatic agenda of deregulation and state retrenchment (Harvey, 2005; Mirowski & Plehwe, 2009; Plehwe, 2014). This diffusion accounts for the availability of a ready-made anti-statist repertoire to political actors far removed from the contexts in which these ideas were originally elaborated.

This is not, however, the only way in which expert-guided governance is contested. A different strand ofRecent scholarship has further suggested that contemporary populist movements increasingly challenge not only specific public policies but also the institutions responsible for producing authoritative knowledge and informing public decision-making (Jasanoff, 2004, 2011; Fischer, 2009; Weingart, 1999). Public universities, scientific agencies, expert bureaucracies, and regulatory institutions become associated with technocratic elites whose authority is portrayed as politically biased, ideologically captured, or disconnected from ordinary citizens. The two logics are distinct, as one denies the state's competence to act upon knowledge, the other denies the credibility of the knowledge itself, yet they are politically complementary, since together they deprive expert-informed public action of both an epistemic and an institutional foundation. The Milei administration appears to combine them (Merke, 2026), which is why the framework developed below treats the delegitimization of state intervention and the delegitimization of public expertise as separate analytical dimensions.In this context, opposition extends beyond individual policies towards broader challenges to the legitimacy of public expertise and state-coordinated governance. The Milei administration appears to deepen this tendency (Merke, 2026).

This discussion suggests that libertarian populism may provide a distinctive ideological foundation for contesting sustainability governance. Rather than focusing exclusively on environmental policy, it raises broader questions about the legitimacy of state intervention, public expertise, and regulatory governance. However, while the literature helps explain these ideological foundations, it provides less insight into the institutional mechanisms through which such ideological projects reshape the state itself. The following section therefore examines the literature on policy dismantling to understand how political ideas are translated into institutional change.

## 2.3 Policy dismantling: from ideological projects to institutional change

While the literature on sustainability-policy backlash explains why governments may oppose climate and environmental policies, it pays comparatively less attention to how these political projects are translated into institutional change. This question has been extensively examined within the literature on policy dismantling, which studies the reduction, removal, or weakening of existing public policies and institutions (Bauer et al., 2012; Bauer & Knill, 2014).

The most developed account of how governments reduce public intervention is found in the literature on policy dismantling. Policy dismantling is commonly defined as a deliberate process through which governments reduce the density, intensity, or scope of public policies, either by removing policy instruments, reducing resources, weakening implementation, or reorganizing the institutions responsible for policy delivery (Bauer et al., 2012). Importantly, dismantling does not necessarily imply the complete abolition of policies. Governments may instead pursue more gradual or less visible strategies, including budget reductions, organizational restructuring, administrative simplification, deregulation, or the weakening of implementation and enforcement capacities (Green-Pedersen, 2002; Jordan, Bauer, & Green-Pedersen, 2013). Consequently, policy change often occurs through cumulative institutional adjustments rather than through highly visible legislative reforms.

Retrenchment is politically costly. The dismantling literature has also highlighted the political constraints associated with retrenchment. Because removing public policies often generates electoral costs and opposition from affected stakeholders, governments frequently adopt strategies that minimize political conflict, including incremental reforms, organizational mergers, delegation, or reductions in administrative capacity rather than outright policy repeal (Green-Pedersen, 2002; Bauer et al., 2012). Such approaches allow governments to reshape the functioning of the state while maintaining formal policy commitments or avoiding direct political confrontation.

IRecent institutional scholarship further suggests that significant policy change frequently occurs through gradual transformations rather than abrupt institutional rupture (Mahoney & Thelen, 2010; Streeck & Thelen, 2005). Institutional conversion, displacement, layering, or drift may progressively alter the objectives and functioning of public organizations without requiring comprehensive legislative reform (sumar ref del de los varones de roll back). These perspectives broaden the understanding of dismantling beyond the removal of individual policy instruments and highlight the importance of administrative and organizational change in explaining long-term institutional transformation.

Although this literature provides important insights into the mechanisms through which governments retrench public intervention, its primary focus has remained on policy outputs and institutional reform. Comparatively less attention has been devoted to the implications of dismantling for the broader capacities of the state to govern complex societal transitions. This distinction is particularly relevant in the field of sustainability, where effective governance depends not only on the existence of environmental policies but also on the fiscal resources, administrative capabilities, regulatory institutions, scientific expertise, and coordination mechanisms required to design, implement, monitor, and adapt those policies over time. Understanding the consequences of policy dismantling therefore requires complementing this literature with scholarship on policy and state capacities.

## 2.4 State capacities for sustainability governance

Policy dismantling concerns not only the reduction of existing policy instruments but also the weakening of the institutional resources through which governments formulate and pursue collective objectives. This broader consequence can be examined through the literature on state and policy capacity. While state capacity generally refers to the ability of public authorities to formulate objectives and implement them effectively, policy capacity focuses more specifically on the competencies and resources required to perform policy functions, from producing knowledge and designing interventions to coordinating actors and enforcing decisions. The two concepts overlap, but policy capacity directs attention to the concrete organizational foundations of specific government action rather than treating the state as a unitary actor.

A particularly influential framework defines policy capacity as the combination of skills and resources required for effective policymaking and distinguishes among analytical, operational, and political capacities operating at the individual, organizational, and systemic levels (Wu et al., 2015). Analytical capacity concerns the ability to generate, interpret, and apply scientific and technical knowledge, evaluate policy alternatives, and support evidence-informed decision-making. Operational capacity refers to the organizational resources needed to design, coordinate, administer, monitor, and enforce public policies. Political capacity encompasses the ability to build legitimacy, coordinate stakeholders, manage conflict, and sustain political support for collective action. These dimensions are mutually reinforcing: analytical knowledge has limited influence without organizations capable of acting upon it, while administrative resources are unlikely to be effective without the political capacity to mobilize support and coordinate across institutions.

This perspective is particularly relevant for sustainability governance. Environmental and climate challenges are characterized by long-term time horizons, scientific uncertainty, cross-sectoral interdependencies, and conflicts over the distribution of costs and benefits. As a result, governing sustainability requires considerably more than adopting individual regulations or setting formal policy targets. It depends on the state's ability to produce and mobilize scientific knowledge, monitor environmental change, formulate long-term strategies, coordinate across ministries and levels of government, engage societal actors, enforce regulatory standards, and adapt policies over time (Lemos & Agrawal, 2006). Research on adaptive climate governance similarly emphasizes that responding to complex environmental problems requires the simultaneous development of analytical, administrative, and political capacities rather than reliance on any single governance instrument (Jordan & Huitema, 2014).

The capacity perspective therefore provides an important complement to the policy dismantling literature. A policy may formally remain in force while the state's ability to implement it gradually deteriorates. Budget reductions can weaken monitoring systems, scientific research, inspections, and programme delivery; organizational restructuring may fragment responsibilities and erode institutional memory; and the downgrading or elimination of specialized agencies can undermine coordination and technical expertise. Likewise, weakening public research institutions or scientific advisory bodies reduces the knowledge infrastructure upon which evidence-based policymaking depends (Jasanoff, 2004). In such contexts, governments may preserve formal policy commitments while simultaneously diminishing the institutional capacities necessary to achieve them.

Capacity erosion should therefore not be understood merely as the unintended consequence of fiscal constraints or administrative inefficiency. Rather, it may result from deliberate political choices regarding which functions the state should perform, which forms of expertise are regarded as legitimate, and which public institutions should retain authority and resources. This understanding is consistent with broader scholarship on the selective restructuring of the state, which emphasizes that governments often strengthen certain capacities while intentionally reducing others in accordance with changing political and ideological priorities (Jessop, 2002). This observation directly connects the capacity literature with the ideological dynamics discussed in the preceding sections. When public intervention, environmental regulation, or scientific expertise are portrayed as inherently inefficient, coercive, or illegitimate, reducing the capacities that sustain them may be presented not as a governance failure but as a political achievement. From this perspective, the weakening of state capacities can constitute an intended outcome of an anti-statist governing project rather than an unintended by-product of fiscal adjustment.

Taken together, these four strands of literature provide important but partial explanations of the contemporary transformation of sustainability governance. Research on sustainability backlash explains the growing political resistance to climate and environmental policies, while studies of libertarian populism illuminate the ideological narratives through which state intervention and scientific expertise are challenged. The literature on policy dismantling identifies the institutional mechanisms through which governments reshape public policies, and the state capacity perspective highlights the broader governance consequences of these reforms. However, these perspectives have largely evolved in parallel, offering limited guidance on how ideological narratives become translated into institutional change. To address this gap, the following section develops an analytical framework that conceptualizes anti-statist sustainability backlash as a dual process combining discursive delegitimization and institutional erosion.

# **3\. An Analytical Framework for Anti-statist Sustainability Backlash**

## 3.1 Anti-statist sustainability backlash: a dual-process framework

Building on the preceding discussion, we conceptualize anti-statist sustainability backlash as a dual process through which libertarian ideas are translated into transformations of sustainability governance. Rather than understanding backlash solely as opposition to particular environmental policies, we argue that anti-statist sustainability backlash simultaneously seeks to undermine the legitimacy of sustainability governance and to weaken the institutional capacities through which governments pursue sustainability objectives.

The framework distinguishes between two analytically distinct but mutually reinforcing dimensions: discursive delegitimization and institutional erosion**.** The first captures the narratives through which sustainability governance is portrayed as politically, scientifically, or culturally illegitimate. The second captures the institutional changes that reduce the state's capacity to formulate, coordinate, implement, monitor, and adapt sustainability policies. Together, these dimensions explain how ideological opposition to sustainability can become embedded in governmental institutions and administrative practice.

While analytically distinct, the two dimensions are closely interconnected. Discursive delegitimization provides the political and ideological justification for institutional reforms, whereas institutional erosion reduces the state's ability to sustain and defend public action on sustainability over time. This interaction creates a self-reinforcing dynamic in which weakening institutions further diminish the capacity to generate scientific knowledge, coordinate public policies, and maintain long-term sustainability governance. The following sections elaborate each dimension in greater detail.

## 3.2 Discursive delegitimization

The first dimension captures how governmental discourse challenges the legitimacy of sustainability governance by questioning its institutional, epistemic, and normative foundations. Rather than focusing on disagreement over specific environmental measures, this dimension examines broader narratives that redefine the role of the state, the authority of scientific expertise, and the societal legitimacy of sustainability itself. These narratives create a political environment in which institutional reforms can be justified as restoring freedom, reducing bureaucracy, or eliminating ideological bias. Three interrelated forms of discursive delegitimization are distinguished.

The first concerns the delegitimization of the state's role in sustainability governance. Here, public intervention is portrayed as inefficient, coercive, or incompatible with individual liberty and market competition. Environmental regulation, state planning, and multilateral environmental cooperation are framed not as legitimate instruments for addressing collective problems but as unjustified constraints on economic freedom and private initiative. The object of contestation is therefore not only individual policies but the broader legitimacy of state involvement in sustainability governance.

The second concerns the delegitimization of public science and expertise. Sustainability governance relies heavily on scientific knowledge, technical expertise, and specialized public institutions capable of informing policymaking under conditions of uncertainty. Anti-statist discourse frequently challenges these institutions by portraying scientists, universities, public research organizations, and technical experts as politically biased, ideologically captured, or disconnected from society. Such narratives weaken the authority of expert knowledge as a legitimate basis for collective decision-making and contribute to the erosion of trust in public institutions responsible for producing and mobilizing scientific evidence.

The third concerns the cultural delegitimization of sustainability. Rather than treating climate and environmental policies as responses to ecological challenges, sustainability is embedded within broader ideological conflicts surrounding culture, identity, and political values. Environmental governance is associated with wider narratives concerning "wokeism," globalism, socialism, or progressive cultural agendas, transforming sustainability from a policy domain into a symbol of broader political confrontation. This cultural reframing broadens opposition beyond specific environmental policies and positions sustainability governance as part of a wider ideological project.

Taken together, these three forms of delegitimization target the institutional, epistemic, and normative pillars upon which sustainability governance is built. Rather than representing independent narratives, they collectively contribute to redefining sustainability governance as politically illegitimate and therefore as an appropriate object of institutional reform.

## 3.3 Institutional erosion

The second dimension focuses on the institutional consequences of anti-statist sustainability backlash. Building on the literature on policy dismantling and state capacities, we define institutional erosion as the progressive weakening of the capacities that enable governments to formulate, coordinate, implement, enforce, monitor, and adapt sustainability policies. The emphasis is therefore not solely on whether particular regulations are formally abolished, but on whether the institutional infrastructure required for effective sustainability governance is preserved or weakened.

For the purposes of this article, state capacities for sustainability governance refer to the institutional, financial, administrative, regulatory, coordinative, and knowledge-based resources that enable public authorities to pursue long-term sustainability objectives. This conception extends beyond the implementation of individual policies to encompass the broader organizational and epistemic foundations that make sustained public action possible.

Institutional erosion may occur through several interconnected mechanisms. Budgetary retrenchment reduces the financial and human resources available to organizations responsible for sustainability governance, limiting their ability to perform regulatory, scientific, and administrative functions. Institutional downgrading weakens the authority, autonomy, specialization, or coordinating role of ministries, agencies, and public research institutions responsible for sustainability governance. Finally, policy dismantling reduces or removes regulations, programmes, planning instruments, and implementation arrangements that support sustainability objectives. Although analytically distinguishable, these mechanisms frequently reinforce one another. Reduced budgets weaken organizational performance; institutional restructuring fragments responsibilities and erodes institutional memory; and the dismantling of policies further diminishes the political justification for maintaining specialized governance capacities.

The framework does not assume that anti-statist governments seek to reduce state capacity in general. Rather, it examines the selective erosion of those state capacities associated with sustainability governance, while other governmental functions may be maintained or even strengthened. This distinction is particularly important for understanding contemporary anti-statist projects, which often combine a reduced role for the regulatory and environmental state with the reinforcement of other state functions.

**Figure 1** summarizes the analytical framework proposed in this article, illustrating how libertarian ideas are translated into institutional changes through the interaction between discursive delegitimization and institutional erosion.

# **4\. Empirical Research Design** 

This article adopts a single-case, explanatory research design to examine how anti-statist sustainability backlash is articulated through political discourse and manifested in changes to the institutional capacities underpinning sustainability governance. Argentina under Javier Milei provides a theoretically relevant case because the government has explicitly challenged the legitimacy of environmental governance, scientific institutions, and state intervention while simultaneously implementing extensive institutional reforms. Rather than aiming for statistical generalization, the study seeks analytical generalization by examining whether and how the empirical patterns observed in the Argentine case refine the conceptual framework developed in Section 3\.

Consistent with the dual-process framework developed in Section 3, the empirical strategy triangulates two independently but complementary data sources. Corpus A consists of Javier Milei's presidential speeches and public discourses and is examined through abductive qualitative content analysis to identify patterns of discursive delegitimization (Dimension 1). Corpus B consists of formal governmental documentation \-including executive decrees, budgetary records, and organizational and regulatory documents- supplemented where appropriate by secondary documentary evidence, and is designed to trace state capability erosion (Dimension 2\) through budgetary retrenchment, administrative restructuring, and changes to sustainability-policy instruments. The remainder of this section details the construction of the two corpora, the analytical procedures applied to each, and the strategy used to integrate their findings.

## 4.1 Data collection

### *4.1.1 Corpus A: presidential speeches and public discourses*

Corpus A consists of the population of publicly available presidential speeches formally transcribed and published by the Casa Rosada between 10 December 2023 and 29 April 2026, supplemented by his 8 October 2023 presidential debate \-included as it establishes the pre-inauguration baseline for Milei's climate-related rhetoric immediately prior to assuming office. The corpus was assembled and is maintained in a master tracking database recording, for each event, its date, venue, country, event type, and the source URL. Full verbatim transcripts were collected primarily by scraping the entirety of Casa Rosada's official speeches registry to build an exhaustive index of every recorded Milei speech as President. Each transcript was saved as a structured text file preserving frontmatter metadata and the full, raw body text. Speeches were preserved in their original language (predominantly Spanish, with a subset of internationally hosted addresses transcribed in English by their host institution).

The final corpus totals 193 distinct speech events (10 December 2023 \- 29 April 2026, plus the 8 October 2023 presidential debate) spanning 6 event-type categories in 14 countries. Two-thirds of the corpus (66.8%) was delivered domestically, with the United States, Israel, and Spain accounting for the largest foreign-venue concentrations. Table X summarizes corpus composition.

### *4.1.2 Corpus B: formal documentation*

The second empirical component assembles Corpus B from formal governmental documentation: national budget laws and execution reports, executive decrees (particularly the delegated-powers deregulation packages of December 2023 and July 2025), ministerial reorganization resolutions and official-gazette organizational charts, and environmental and mining regulatory instruments (e.g., the RIGI large-investment incentive regime). ## 4.2 Data analysis

### *Analytical approach*

The analysis of Corpus A followed an abductive coding strategy, combining a theory-informed deductive coding framework with iterative refinement through engagement with the empirical material, thus evolving throughout the analytical process (Braun et al. 2019). A first set of deductive "seed" categories was derived from the conceptual framework developed in Section 3; followed by an inductive process of refining, merging, or adding categories where the data revealed new patterns (CITATION). The unit of analysis is the rhetorical passage (typically a paragraph) coded for the presence of one or more of the categories described below. The focus on speeches by President Javier Milei reflects the highly personalized and leader-centered nature of the current Argentine government and the broader political movement that has emerged around Milei, in which presidential discourse constitutes the primary vehicle for articulating ideological positions, legitimizing policy choices, and framing public debate. 

### *Codebook development*

Following non-positivists qualitative principles, the abductive orientation was operationalized by designing an inherently recursive and iterative codebook development process rather than a linear trajectory (Byrne, 2022; Braun & Clarke, 2019). The procedure combined theory-informed deductive categories with systematic refinement based on their application to a benchmark corpus. The purpose of the iteration was to progressively improve the conceptual fit, distinctiveness, and operational clarity of the coding scheme before applying it to the full corpus.

The codebook underwent multiple cycles of inductive expansion, deductive refinement, and category consolidation. Specifically, it was developed through four successive versions (v1–v4). Versions v1–v3 were piloted exclusively on a benchmark subset of flagship speeches (e.g., the WEF Davos addresses, the UN General Assembly speeches, and the Legislative Session Openings). The iterative process operated at two levels: empirical iteration, whereby engagement with the speeches revealed recurrent patterns not fully anticipated by the initial framework; and procedural iteration, whereby coding rules and decision criteria were refined to improve consistency and reduce interpretive ambiguity. Version v4 was the result of a peer-reviewed researchers team,  was progressively scaled in batches of 5 to the full set of 193 speech events. This benchmark-first strategy allowed conceptual categories to be evaluated against the empirical material, with categories being refined, merged, renamed, promoted, or discarded as the analysis progressed. The initial application also allowed potentially recurrent patterns not anticipated in the deductive framework to be recorded as provisional inductive categories, providing candidates for subsequent testing.

### *Coding execution and “Human-Designed-and-Managed Loop” (Nguyen-Trung & Friese, 2026\)*

Once the v4 codebook had been finalized through human peer review, it was applied to the full corpus using a human-managed AI-assisted coding process. The purpose of this stage was to combine the scalability of large language models with continued human control over the interpretation and application of the coding framework. Crucially, the integration of Large Language Models into the coding pipeline was structured to preserve this qualitative recursivity through a “human-designed-and-managed loop” (Nguyen-Trung & Friese, 2026). Because automated LLM workflows risk imposing a rigid, linear pass over text without genuine interpretive comparison, we embedded AI-assisted annotation within an iterative, four-version codebook development process (v1 → v4). Each codebook version was calibrated against benchmark texts, subjected to line-by-line human peer review, and audited for overcoding and boundary ambiguities prior to corpus-wide application. In this way, the LLM functioned as an interlocutor for systematic pattern retrieval, while human researchers drove the recursive refinement of the analytical categories.

The full-corpus application proceeded incrementally in batches of five speeches. For each batch, the model was provided with the complete v4 codebook and coding instructions and generated coded versions of the five transcripts. The researchers then manually reviewed the resulting annotations before the next batch was processed. This review did not merely assess whether the model had followed the existing instructions; it also identified ambiguities in category boundaries, instances of overcoding or undercoding, and passages for which the application of the codebook required clarification. By dividing the full-corpus execution into discrete, human-audited iterations, the workflow accommodated the technical limitations of LLM processing while maintaining continuous human oversight (Nguyen-Trung & Friese, 2026). The coding protocol and model instructions were consequently refined where necessary, and the resulting decisions were incorporated into the instructions used for subsequent batches.

The process thus constituted a feedback loop between machine-assisted execution and human analytical review:

CHART: Human coding → LLM coding → human review → identification of errors and ambiguities → refinement of coding instructions → subsequent LLM coding.

This procedure was repeated iteratively during the initial batches until the application of the stabilized v4 framework became sufficiently consistent to permit systematic scaling. Importantly, these refinements did not constitute new versions of the theoretical codebook unless they altered the definition, scope, or structure of a category. They primarily concerned the operationalization and application of an already established coding framework. This distinction preserves the separation between the earlier abductive development of the codebook and its subsequent controlled execution across the corpus.

CLOSING PARAGRAPH

## 4.3 The coding scheme

The coding scheme is organized around three overarching narrative categories, comprising fourteen sub-codes (Table X). More detailed definitions and examples of each sub-dimension are found in Annex X.

Table X. Coding scheme for the narrative analysis

| Narrative category | Illustrative codes |
| ----- | ----- |
| **Delegitimization of state intervention and sustainability governance** | Market primacy and free-market solutions; anti-state and anti-bureaucratic rhetoric; anti-elite narratives ("la casta"); delegitimization of regulation and public coordination; benefits of deregulation; sustainability governance as ideological or economically harmful; rejection of multilateral (environmental) governance. |
| **Delegitimization of science and expertise** | Criticism of research institutions and universities; attacks on experts and technocratic elites; climate skepticism; dismissal of environmental science; references to "pseudo-science" or ideological science; delegitimization of scientific and professional institutions; rejection of expert mediation in policymaking; selective empiricism. |
| **Cultural backlash narratives** | Anti-socialism and anti-"neo-Marxism"; "woke" narratives; civilizational defense; freedom as a central political principle |

For the analysis of institutional erosion, we did….

The second analytical component examines whether these narratives are accompanied by institutional changes affecting the state's capacity to govern sustainability transitions. Rather than relying on qualitative coding, this stage consists of a structured documentary analysis mapping changes in three dimensions of state capabilities: (i) budgetary, (ii) administrative, and (iii) regulatory (Table 3). Evidence was collected from official budget documents, executive decrees, legislation, governmental organizational charts, ministerial resolutions, and policy documents.

**Table 3\. Operationalization of state capability erosion**

| Dimension | Indicators | Primary sources |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Budgetary capacity | Budget reductions affecting science, environment and sustainability programmes | National Budget, Ministry of Economy, Budget execution reports |
| Administrative capacity | Ministry restructuring, agency mergers or closures, staffing reductions | Executive decrees, organizational charts, official gazettes |
| Regulatory capacity | Changes in environmental regulations, climate commitments and policy instruments | Laws, decrees, NDCs, environmental policy documents |

## 4.3 Analytical strategy

The analysis proceeds in three stages. First, discursive delegitimization is examined through governmental narratives. Second, institutional reforms are analysed according to the framework of institutional erosion. Third, both dimensions are interpreted together to assess whether discursive narratives are accompanied by institutional changes that weaken state capacities for sustainability governance. The objective is not to establish deterministic causality but to assess whether discursive delegitimization and institutional transformation constitute mutually reinforcing dimensions of sustainability-policy dismantling.

# **5\. Findings**

## 5.1. Discursive delegitimization

Across the complete corpus of 193 speeches and public discourses delivered by Javier Milei as presidential candidate and President of Argentina (8 October 2023 \- 29 April 2026), the discursive-delegitimization framework (Dimension 1\) identifies 597 codeable passages: 62.8% of codes target the legitimacy of state intervention and sustainability governance in the abstract (D1.1) rather than scientific knowledge and climate science itself (D1.2, 8.7%), or invoke cultural-backlash framing (D1.3, 28.5%).

| *(A) ![][image1]* D1.1. State Intervention & Governance. D1.2. Public Science & Expertise. D1.3. Cultural Backlash | *(B) ![][image2]* |
| :---: | ----- |

### ***Figure X. Coded passages by dimension (A) & Frequency ranking by subcode (B).***

This is our central finding: Milei's climate obstruction discourse is overwhelmingly institutional and economic-theoretical rather than scientific-denialist. Explicit climate-science denial appears in only three speeches across two and a half years, while the anti-state, anti-"casta", and anti-regulatory discursive infrastructure constitutes the load-bearing apparatus that climate-specific attacks plug into whenever they do appear. We present the three sub-dimensions in descending order of frequency.

### ***5.1.1 Delegitimization of State Intervention and Sustainability Governance (62.8%, 375 codes)***

Anti\_Casta (116) is the single most frequent sub-code in the entire corpus, ahead of Anti\_Socialism\_Anti\_Collectivism (102). Together with Anti\_State\_Anti\_Bureaucratic (92) and Delegitimization\_of\_Regulation (84), these three generic sub-codes account for 49% of the whole corpus. This is the discourse's centre of gravity: a constantly repeated narrative that state institutions, whichever policy domain they administer, are captured by a self-serving political class or are inherently parasitic bureaucratic drag. Environmental and scientific agencies are not condemned as a special case; they are absorbed into a pre-existing and much larger anti-institutional frame. 

Delegitimization\_of\_Regulation (84, 14.1%) and Market\_Primacy (35, 5.9%) supply the theoretical apparatus: the flagship claim, delivered across three consecutive Davos addresses (2024, 2025, 2026\) is that "market failures do not exist":

*\[If transactions are voluntary, the only context in which there can be a market failure is if there is coercion. And the only one with the capacity to coerce in a generalized way is the state, which holds the monopoly of violence. Market failures do not exist.\] \- Davos, 17 January 2024\.*

Environmental externalities are the paradigm case of market failure in environmental economics, and the entire regulatory apparatus of carbon pricing, emissions standards and pollution control rests on the concept. Declaring market failure as logically impossible eliminates the justification for environmental regulation at the level of first principles, without requiring any argument about climate science.

Addressing the United Nations General Assembly in September 2024, Milei described the 2030 Agenda as *"nothing more than a supranational government program, socialist in nature, which seeks to solve the problems of modernity with solutions that violate the sovereignty of nation states and violate people's right to life, liberty and property”*, and the World Economic Forum as promoting *"ridiculous policies … with Malthusian blinders on — such as 'Zero Emission' policies — which harm poor countries in particular"*. Two months later, at the G20, he was blunter still: *"if this is about limiting countries' right to freely exploit their natural resources, do not count on us"*. The register recurs domestically, where environmentalism is named as *"anti-development"* (La Derecha Fest, July 2025\) and, by April 2026, as the *"Green Agenda"* held responsible alongside abortion and immigration for Europe's demographic collapse. These are the passages where the abstract anti-statist apparatus is pointed at named environmental institutions, agreements and policies.

### ***5.1.2 Cultural Backlash (27.7%, 170 codes)***

(OPENING SENTENCE)

Civilizational\_Defense (27 codes, 15.9% of D1.3) establishes the frame within which every other cultural claim is made: politics is a battle for the survival of the West and for the values of freedom that made it prosperous. The frame is announced in the opening sentence of the government's first major international address — "the West is in danger, and it is in danger because those who are supposed to defend the values of the West find themselves co-opted by a worldview that inexorably leads to socialism, and therefore to poverty" (World Economic Forum, Davos, 17 January 2024\) — and is still being restated two years later, when policy is said to be assessed first against "the ethical and moral values that made the West great", defined as "Greek philosophy … Roman law … the rectitude of the Stoics" (Madrid Economic Forum, 14 March 2026).

Anti\_Socialism\_Anti\_Collectivism (102 codes, 60.0% of D1.3, and the second most frequent sub-code in the corpus) names the adversary in that battle and specifies its method: socialism and neo-Marxism have not won by argument but by capturing the institutions that form Western common sense. Milei describes "the cultural hegemony of the left, which intoxicates the great majority of institutions and opinion-formers" (CPAC investors, Mar-a-Lago, 15 November 2024), and, invoking Gramsci explicitly, an operation in which the left "took the media, took culture, took education" and captured "the most prestigious institutions at national and international level" (Cena de la Fundación Faro, Buenos Aires, 13 November 2024). This is what converts a cultural diagnosis into a political programme: if the adversary operates through institutions, then institutions are the legitimate object of attack.

Woke\_Bundling (41 codes, 24.1% of D1.3) is where environmental policy enters the frame, and it enters not on its own account but as one member of the woke agenda, itself presented as socialism's contemporary and more hypocritical form:

\[On this basis wokeism was built, a regime of single thought, sustained by various institutions whose purpose is to penalise dissent: feminism, diversity, inclusion, equity, immigration, abortion, ecologism, gender ideology, among others, are heads of a single creature whose aim is to justify the advance of the State through the appropriation and distortion of noble causes.\] — World Economic Forum, Davos, 23 January 2025\.

The link is made explicit later in the same address: "wokeism is also manifested in sinister radical ecologism and the banner of climate change", where an "elementary idea of preserving the environment" is said to have been perverted into "a fanatical environmentalism in which human beings are a cancer that must be eliminated". The same enumeration recurs domestically — "abortion, radical environmentalism, radical feminism and all the agendas of globalist socialism" (CPAC, Buenos Aires, 5 December 2024).

Read together, the three sub-codes form a single chain of inference. The West is endangered; its institutions have been captured by socialism; wokeism is the form that capture now takes; and ecologism is one of its heads. Environmental governance inherits its illegitimacy from the position assigned to it in a civilizational conflict.

The cultural delegitimization of sustainability, in which environmental governance is detached from ecological problem-solving and relocated inside a wider conflict over identity, values and political order. Its three sub-codes perform three distinct operations.

`Anti_Socialism_Anti_Collectivism` (102 codes, 60.0% of D1.3) is the second most frequent sub-code in the entire corpus, and it establishes the terms of the relocation: environmentalism is not a mistaken response to an ecological problem but a disguised instrument of collectivism, so the objection to it concerns not the environment at all but who acquires power through it. 

**D1.3 functions as a meta-narrative that pre-loads specific arguments with civilizational stakes rather than making an independent case.** Anti\_Socialism\_Anti\_Collectivism (102) is the corpus's second most frequent sub-code overall, appearing across nearly every register. Woke\_Bundling (41) is the mechanism by which climate governance gets contaminated by association with reproductive-rights and gender-ideology framing (examples??). Civilizational\_Defense (27) spans from a generic "the West is in danger" framing (Davos 2024\) to explicit theological grounding.

In global keynotes, climate governance is systematically bundled with progressive social issues (DEI, gender ideology, reproductive rights) and framed as a central front in an existential civilizational conflict against "woke socialism."

### ***5.1.3. Delegitimization of Public Science and Expertise (10.8%, 66 codes)***

Instead of direct climate-science denial, the primary focus of D1.2 is the discursive delegitimization of public expertise and knowledge-producing institutions (Attack\_on\_Experts\_and\_Technocrats, 49.2% of D1.2; Attack\_on\_Universities\_and\_Research\_Institutions, 22.2% of D1.2). The discourse systematically targets the epistemic authority of the experts and institutions that provide the technical rationale for state regulation. When public scientific bodies, universities, or international forums are targeted, these institutions are reframed as centers of "political indoctrination," wasteful rent-seeking, and ideologically captured knowledge production. By characterizing expert communities as nodes in a broader ideological network, the discourse seeks to undermine the epistemic foundation that justifies state planning and environmental monitoring.

Direct climate-science denial (`Climate_Skepticism_or_Dismissal`) accounts for only 1.1% of the corpus. Milei's obstruction is not organised around contesting physical science; the case against environmental regulation is made, as shown above, on economic, institutional, and cultural grounds. Nevertheless, the few instances of explicit denial leave no ambiguity regarding his ideological stance on climate change, which is that climate change is a cyclical, non-human induced phenomenon:

> *\[(...) when one argues that the Earth has already gone through five abrupt temperature-change cycles, and that in four of them man did not even exist, they brand us flat-earthers in order to discredit our ideas, regardless of the fact that science and the data are on our side.\] — World Economic Forum, Davos, 23 January 2025\.*

AGREGAR BREVE PÁRRAFO SELECTIVE EMPIRISM

It is important to note that Milei’s discourse is not anti-science, as he usually supports his claims in science.

### ***5.1.1. Comparing Domestic and International Discursive Strategy***

Milei delivered 129 of the 193 speeches in Argentina and 64 abroad (66.8% and 33.2% of the corpus). While the anti-state narrative (D1.1) predominates in both registers (62.8% of national codes, 59.3% of international ones), the cultural backlash (D1.3) expands markedly abroad, from 24.1% to 33.8% of codes. 

![][image3]

**Figure X.** Sub-code frequency ranking by venue scope.

Remarkably, the leading sub-code changes with the audience. In both registers the leading code designates an enemy, but the enemy is differently constituted. Domestically it is the *casta*: an identifiable class of officeholders and their beneficiaries, whose displacement is the immediate justification for dismantling the state:

> *\[This party of the State is nothing other than a political mega-structure spanning every party label, whose main characteristic is to expropriate wealth from those who work, produce and trade in order to distribute it among themselves, the unions, the social organizations, the actors, the bribed press, the privilege-seeking businessmen and the various supposedly oppressed collectives.\] Cena de la Fundación Faro, Buenos Aires, 13 November 2024\.*

Internationally it is socialism/communism: an ideology with no fixed institutional address, against which the same dismantling is presented as one front in a civilizational conflict (a framing the rise of `Civilizational_Defense` abroad corroborates):

> \[That communism which once appeared under the Soviet flag today shows itself in another guise: it hides behind multiple noble and humanitarian causes, all apparently independent, but intimately linked by a common agenda of war against tradition and hatred of everything we consider good, beautiful and sacred.\] CPAC Budapest, 21 March 2026\.

In sum, Milei names an adversary inside the Argentine state for domestic audiences, and a civilizational conflict for foreign ones, while the underlying case against regulation remains constant.

## 5.2. Institutional erosion

This section relies primarily on official documents, that is, decrees and laws published in the Boletín Oficial, budget laws, and budget execution records from the National Budget Office. Civil-society monitoring (FARN), fact-checkers (Chequeado) and press reports serve as complements. They corroborate the official record, compile series where no consolidated official source exists, and document how each measure was received.

### *5.2.1. Budgetary retrenchment*

Budgetary retrenchment worked through three channels. Nominal budgets were frozen and eroded by inflation, legally mandated funds were left unexecuted, and the 2026 budget formally repealed earmarked financing guarantees. The fiscal context helps explain how this was possible. The government spent its first two years without a budget law. It rolled over the 2023 budget by decree for 2024 (Decree 88/2023) and again for 2025 (Decree 1131/2024). In a high-inflation economy (xx% in 2024, and xx% in 2025), this maximizes executive discretion, because credits frozen at 2023 values lose most of their real value unless the executive deliberately updates them, item by item. The first budget law of the period, Law 27.798 for 2026, was sanctioned on 26 December 2025 and promulgated on 2 January 2026 (Boletín Oficial, 02/01/2026).

Figure X shows the overall result. It compares real executed spending in 2025 with 2023, keeping the 2023 ministerial map constant. This choice neutralizes the effect of the reorganizations described in section 2.2. Total spending by the national administration fell 28.4 percent in real terms. The portfolio of the former Ministry of Environment fell 64.1 percent, that is, 2.3 times deeper than the administration as a whole. The former science portfolio fell 41.6 percent, about 1.5 times the average.

Figure XX. Real change in executed spending by policy portfolio, 2025 versus 2023, on a constant 2023 perimeter. National administration, accrued expenditure (crédito devengado), deflated by IPC INDEC. The dashed line marks the change in total spending (-28.4 percent). 

![][image4]

Source: authors' elaboration based on National Budget Office / Presupuesto Abierto data.

The environmental cut is deep, but it is not the deepest in the budget. Housing and habitat fell 99 percent, and public works fell 79 percent. This means that environment and science were not singled out as one sector among others, but they were defunded as part of a general project of state retrenchment, and they were cut well above that project's budget's average. What sets them apart, as the rest of this section shows, is that deep defunding came together with discursive targeting, institutional downgrading and, in the end, formal legislative rollback. Gender policy followed the same route, its former ministry's portfolio fell 100 percent. The deepest cuts thus converge on the policy domains that the government's cultural-backlash narrative bundles together (see Section 5.1). The result does not depend on how the data are cut. Measured by budget function instead of portfolio, the environment fell 64.7 percent and science 43.9 percent, almost identical figures (Annex Figure A1).

Science was hit well above the average. Its budget fell more than 40 percent in real terms between 2023 and 2025 (Figure X; Annex Figure A1) and is heading toward a cumulative fall of about half under the 2026 budget (CIICTI, 2026). Public investment in science and technology is projected at 0.140 percent of GDP for 2026, the lowest level since 1972 (CIICTI, 2026, based on official budget data). The research-funding agency (Agencia I+D+i) lost 69.1 percent of its real financing in 2024 and 42.4 percent in 2025, and the 2026 budget cuts a further 12.7 percent, an accumulated fall of 84.5 percent in three years (CIICTI, 2026). Doctoral and postdoctoral fellowship cohorts were roughly halved. PICT 2022 research grants that had already been awarded were cancelled (Cronista, 2024; Mongabay, 2026). The 2026 budget also made the retreat formal. Article 30, subsection b, of Law 27.798 repealed articles 5, 6 and 7 of Law 27.614, the science financing law of 2021\. Article 5 set the goal of reaching 1 percent of GDP by 2032\. Article 6 fixed the annual minimum path, with 0.52 percent for 2026\. Article 7 guaranteed that funding would never fall below the previous year in absolute terms. The financing path approved by Congress in 2021 was not just under-implemented. It was legally dismantled.

The 2026 budget deepens the environmental trajectory of Figure X. The Subsecretaría de Ambiente received ARS 51.5 billion for 2026\. That is a further real cut of 33.8 percent against 2025, and of 79.5 percent against 2023 (FARN, 2026). These FARN figures are not directly comparable with Figure X. They refer to budget allocations, not executed spending, and to the Subsecretaría alone, not the full 2023 perimeter. That explains the difference in magnitude. As a share of total national spending, the environmental budget fell from 0.12 percent in 2023 to 0.03 percent in 2026 (FARN, 2026). Execution data confirm the trend. In 2025 the Subsecretaría executed its lowest budget in nine years, almost 70 percent below 2023 in real terms (FARN, 2026), a figure consistent with Figure X. The National Fund for the Conservation of Native Forests shows the same pattern at the level of a single instrument. By law it must receive at least 0.3 percent of the national budget plus 2 percent of agricultural export duties (Law 26.331, art. 31). In 2024 its allocation was between eighteen and twenty-eight times below that legal floor, with near-zero execution (FARN, 2024). In 2025 it executed ARS 2.4 billion, 155 times less than the amount the law mandates (FARN, 2026).

Fire management shows how smaller allocations and discretionary under-execution interact. The National Fire Management Service (SNMF) had ARS 12.1 billion available for 2024\. It executed nothing during the first quarter, in the middle of the fire season, and about 40 percent of its credit by late August (Chequeado, 2024, based on National Budget Office data). Under-execution itself is not new. The rate was 41.9 percent in 2022 and 41.2 percent in 2023\. What changed under this administration is the collapse of real allocations and the dissolution of the earmarked funds behind the policy (see 2.2 and 2.3). The service entered the severe 2025 fire season with no recorded execution in January, while large fires burned in Patagonia and Corrientes (FARN, 2025). Its 2026 allocation is the second lowest in ten years (TN, 2026), within a real cut of about 69 percent for the environmental area against 2023 (FARN, 2026; Chequeado, 2026).

Public universities, a central part of the country's research capacity, suffered deep real cuts in 2024 and a long legislative conflict. The president vetoed university financing laws passed by Congress in 2024 and again in 2025\. In October 2025 Congress overrode the veto for the first time, but the government delayed implementation, invoking the absence of a budget allocation.
