### *5.2.2. Institutional downgrading and administrative restructuring*

The administration's most consequential intervention in sustainability governance was not the repeal of environmental law in itself, but the reorganization of the administrative apparatus that designs, coordinates and enforces it. The government lowered the institutional rank of the environmental, climate and science bureaucracies, scattered their competences across unrelated portfolios, and thinned their staffing. The combined effect is a hollowing-out of state capacity that happens below the threshold of formal legal change.

### **Reorganization and downgrading of ministries and secretariats**

The downgrading began with the government's first normative act. Decree 8/2023 (Boletín Oficial, 11/12/2023), issued the day after the inauguration, amended the Law of Ministries and halved the number of ministries. It eliminated the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development as a cabinet-level body and initially placed its functions under the Ministry of the Interior. Decree 33/2024 (Boletín Oficial, 09/01/2024) then merged the former environment portfolio with Tourism and Sports into a single secretariat, with environment as one of three undersecretariats. In November 2025 that secretariat was transferred to the Chief of Cabinet's Office (Decree 793/2025, Boletín Oficial, 11/11/2025). As of September 2026, the national environmental authority is the Subsecretaría de Ambiente, inside the Secretariat of Tourism and Environment of the Chief of Cabinet's Office (Decree 48/2026, Boletín Oficial, 27/01/2026). In two years the environmental authority descended two full tiers, from ministry to secretariat to undersecretariat. This loss of rank reduces its budgetary autonomy, its convening power over the provinces, and its weight in inter-ministerial coordination.

Public science followed the same path. Decree 8/2023 also eliminated the Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation, which became a secretariat under the Chief of Cabinet's Office. The downgrade matters for sustainability governance because the science system produces the knowledge that climate and environmental policy needs, from emissions inventories to glacier monitoring. It was widely read as a signal of the government's devaluation of public expertise. In March 2024, sixty-eight Nobel laureates sent an open letter of concern about the defunding of Argentine science (Infobae, 2024; El País, 2024).

### **Elimination, merger, and reassignment of agencies**

The restructuring also moved key agencies to portfolios with different missions. Decree 81/2025 (Boletín Oficial, 12/02/2025) transferred the National Fire Management Service out of the environmental area and into the Ministry of Security. Decree 463/2025 later redirected the levy that financed fire management under Law 26.815, a 3 per mille charge on insurance premiums, to the same ministry. Placing fire management inside a security and emergency apparatus weakens its preventive and ecological orientation. A sustainability function is reframed as a public-order function.

The trust funds that gave these policies financial continuity were dissolved by decree. Decree 888/2024 (Boletín Oficial, 08/10/2024) dissolved the native-forests trust fund created in 2018 and sent its resources to the Treasury. The Federal Environment Council (COFEMA), which gathers the provincial environmental authorities, formally rejected the dissolution as unconstitutional and arbitrary (COFEMA, 2024; La Nación, 2024). Decree 463/2025 (Boletín Oficial, 08/07/2025), issued under the delegated powers of article 5 of Law 27.742, dissolved the National Fire Management Fund and two other public trust funds, citing administrative irregularities. ACUMAR, the inter-jurisdictional authority for the Matanza-Riachuelo basin, which serves more than five million people in one of Latin America's most polluted areas, lost more than 300 staff to dismissals and suffered successive budget cuts after the closure of the associated court case (FARN, 2025; Página/12, 2025). The National Parks Administration was moved across jurisdictions in successive reorganizations. Since 2026 it operates inside the Secretariat of Tourism and Environment of the Chief of Cabinet's Office (Decree 48/2026).

### **Changes in regulatory institutions**

Two horizontal instruments framed the whole restructuring. The emergency mega-decree of deregulation (DNU 70/2023, Boletín Oficial, 21/12/2023) and the delegated powers of the "Bases" law (Law 27.742, art. 5\) authorized the executive to reorganize, merge or dissolve public bodies and trust funds. As the dissolutions above show, those powers were used against environmental institutions. Decree 90/2025 (Boletín Oficial, 17/02/2025) added a standing instruction to every national public body, streamline procedures and eliminate regulations considered to generate unnecessary costs. Civil-society organizations argued that this permanent deregulation mandate, applied to environmental protection, violates the non-regression principle of the Escazú Agreement, ratified by Law 27.566 (FARN, 2025). The deeper point is that the capacity to issue, monitor and enforce rules became more discretionary and more dependent on political will.

### **Staffing reductions and administrative hollowing-out**

Staffing cuts completed the picture. Official reports by the Ministry of Deregulation and State Transformation count more than 60,000 positions eliminated from the national administration and state enterprises between December 2023 and mid-2026. The official target for 2026 is a further cut of 10 percent of the workforce, about 27,000 positions (Ministerio de Desregulación y Transformación del Estado, in La Nación, 2026; Infobae, 2026). The science system was among the hardest hit. CONICET, the country's main scientific institution, lost about 2,650 positions between June 2023 and mid-2026, including 2,027 doctoral and postdoctoral fellows and 623 researchers and support staff. The real salaries of its researchers fell 40.4 percent in the same period (CIICTI, 2026, based on official records). The wider public science system, which includes CONICET, the atomic energy commission (CNEA), the meteorological service (SMN), INTI and INTA, lost about 6,400 posts by August 2026 (Grupo EPC; CIICTI, 2026). These bodies run the monitoring networks and hold the technical expertise behind climate and environmental policy. Their attrition directly reduces the state's ability to plan, monitor and enforce, even where legal mandates remain untouched.

### *5.2.3 Sustainability-policy dismantling*

The government also dismantled sustainability policy itself. It did so through three routes: disengagement from international climate governance, defunding of key domestic instruments, and deregulation aimed at environmental-protection law. During the first two years this happened almost without formal repeal. The framework climate law and Argentina's international commitments stayed formally in force while the capacity to implement them shrank. This changed in late 2025\. Once the October 2025 midterm elections strengthened the government's coalition in Congress, dismantling extended to formal legislative rollback. Its clearest expression is the April 2026 reform of the Glacier Protection Law, the first substantive weakening of a minimum-standards environmental law since that legal category was created.

**Changes in climate targets and international commitments**

The retreat from climate commitments was announced at the highest level. In November 2024 the foreign minister, Gerardo Werthein, said the government was re-evaluating its whole climate-negotiation strategy (TN, 2024; Clarín, 2024). In February 2025, shortly after announcing the exit from the World Health Organization, President Milei said he was considering withdrawing from the Paris Agreement and called the environmental agenda "a fraud" (Infobae, 2025; La Nación, 2025). Withdrawal never happened. The agreement had been ratified by Congress (Law 27.270), and the government finally chose permanence with minimal commitment. In November 2025, days before COP30, Argentina presented its third Nationally Determined Contribution, prepared within the National Climate Change Cabinet created by Law 27.520 (Gobierno de la Argentina, 2025; UNFCCC, 2025). NDC 3.0 sets a single emissions cap of 375 MtCO2e for both 2030 and 2035\. The previous update, in 2021, had committed to a lower cap of 349 MtCO2e for 2030\. The government presented the higher number as a methodological revision. It cited wider territorial coverage (from 65 to 79 percent), more emission categories (from 146 to 162\) and updated IPCC metrics, and called the new targets "achievable and realistic" (Gobierno de la Argentina, 2025). Independent analysts read it differently. A flat cap through 2035 means no additional mitigation effort for a decade, an ambition downgrade in all but name (FARN, 2025; Círculo de Políticas Ambientales, 2025). 

**Selective disengagement from international climate governance**

The clearest act of disengagement came at COP29 in Baku, in November 2024\. On the third day of negotiations the government ordered its accredited delegation, about eighty-five people, to leave (Climática, 2024; El Economista, 2024). Observers called the move unprecedented in Argentine diplomatic history and a sharp break with the country's tradition of active participation in climate negotiations (La Nación, 2024). It was widely read as part of a foreign-policy realignment toward the incoming Trump administration, together with a pattern of isolated or contrarian votes in multilateral fora (FARN, 2024). A year later, Argentina did attend COP30 in Belém, but minimally. It sent about five officials, headed by a Foreign Ministry director, after the Chief of Cabinet refused to authorize the environment undersecretary's trip. The delegation kept a marginal profile, which observers described as nearly irrelevant. It also refused to endorse gender-related language in negotiated texts, in line with the government's cultural agenda (Chequeado, 2025; Infobae, 2025; La Nación, 2025).

**Changes in key policy instruments**

Key policy instruments were neutralized in practice without being repealed. The National Fund for the Conservation of Native Forests survives on paper. Its legally mandated funding is ignored and its trust-fund vehicle was dissolved (Decree 888/2024; FARN, 2024, 2026; see 2.1). Fire management lost both its earmarked fund, dissolved by Decree 463/2025, and its institutional home, transferred to the Ministry of Security by Decree 81/2025. The climate-governance architecture of Law 27.520, including the National Climate Change Cabinet, formally still exists. In each case the instrument survives in name while losing the funding, rank and administrative support it needs to work.

**Deregulation affecting environmental protection**

Deregulation advanced through successive vehicles. The first version of the "Bases" bill, in December 2023, proposed regressive amendments to three minimum-standards laws, on native forests (Law 26.331), glaciers (Law 26.639) and open burning (Law xx). Civil-society and scientific resistance forced those chapters out, and the law enacted in July 2024 had no environmental chapter (Ámbito, 2023; FARN, 2024). But the enacted law created the Large Investment Incentive Regime (RIGI), which grants thirty-year fiscal, customs and exchange-rate privileges to large investments, mainly in mining, oil and gas. FARN and other organizations warned about three features of the regime. It requires no environmental-impact assessment and no cumulative-impact evaluation. It exempts investments from layers of national, provincial and municipal regulation. And it coexists with delegated powers that allow the executive to shrink or dissolve environmental agencies (FARN, 2024; EcoNews, 2024; Agencia TSS, 2025). Decree 90/2025 then generalized the deregulatory mandate across the administration, and FARN invoked the non-regression principle of the Escazú Agreement against it (FARN, 2025).

### **From erosion to formal rollback: the 2026 reform of the Glacier Law**

The reform of the Glacier Protection Law is the clearest completed sequence from discursive delegitimization to formal policy change. On 13 November 2025, at a regional economic congress in Corrientes, Milei announced a "periglacial law" that would let each province determine its own periglacial zones. He framed environmentalist opposition as a preference that people "starve rather than touch anything" (see Section 5.1). On 15 December 2025 the executive sent the bill to Congress for extraordinary sessions (Diario de Cuyo, 2025). The Senate approved it, and the Chamber of Deputies gave final sanction on 8 April 2026, by 137 votes to 111 with 3 abstentions. The executive promulgated it as Law 27.804 on 24 April 2026 (Decree 271/2026, Boletín Oficial, 24/04/2026). The new law ends the automatic protection that Law 26.639 had given to glaciers and the periglacial environment since 2010\. Protection now covers only bodies with a proven hydrological function, determined and delimited by each province. Previously restricted periglacial areas are open to mining (Law 27.804; Chequeado, 2026; Infobae, 2026). CONICET glaciologists at IANIGLA, the institute that produces the national glacier inventory, opposed the reform, together with broad scientific and civil-society coalitions (Mongabay, 2026; FARN, 2026).

The glacier reform matters for our argument in three ways. First, it is the first time Congress substantively weakened a minimum-standards environmental law since the category exists. Dismantling moved from budgets and organizational charts to formal legislation. Second, the sequence is unusually clean. The presidential announcement of November 2025, coded in Corpus A as the most direct bridge between rhetoric and policy, became a statute in five months. Discursive delegitimization prepared a concrete dismantling outcome. Third, the timing supports our expectation about political opportunity. While the government lacked votes in Congress, dismantling advanced through erosion and circumvention. Once the October 2025 midterms strengthened its coalition, formal rollback became possible and happened at once. 

### **Reduced implementation and enforcement of existing policies**

The gap between formal commitments and real capacity is most visible in enforcement. 2025 was an especially destructive fire year, with about 40 percent more burned area than 2024 (Chequeado, 2026, based on official fire statistics). Yet the fire service entered that season with no recorded execution in January and works with a 2026 allocation that is the second lowest in ten years (FARN, 2025; TN, 2026). The native-forest fund went similarly unexecuted amid the broader collapse of environmental funding (FARN, 2026; Chequeado, 2026). The weakening of ACUMAR reduced enforcement in the Matanza-Riachuelo basin (FARN, 2025; Página/12, 2025).

Taken together, these developments illustrate our central claim. Dismantling followed a clear trajectory. Erosion and circumvention came first, through under-execution, defunding, downgrading and reassignment, while formal frameworks endured. Outright legal rollback followed when the political opportunity arrived, as the glacier reform shows. The recurrent targets, forest, glacier and fire legislation, are precisely the laws that limit extractive expansion. In each domain, obligations that remain on paper are stripped of the administrative, fiscal and technical capacity needed to fulfil them. Formal permanence with material incapacitation is the defining signature of capability erosion as a mode of sustainability-policy dismantling.

# **6\. Discussion & Conclusion**

**6.1 Anti-statist sustainability backlash: from discourse to institutional change**

The findings identify a form of sustainability backlash that differs in important respects from the climate obstructionism emphasized in much of the existing literature. Research on climate denial and obstruction has documented how political and economic actors contest climate science, manufacture uncertainty, and delay regulatory intervention (McCright & Dunlap, 2000; Jacques et al., 2008; Oreskes & Conway, 2010; Brulle, 2014; Dunlap & McCright, 2015). Explicit climate-science denial is also present in Milei's discourse, including rejection of the anthropogenic character of climate change, but it is quantitatively marginal. The dominant argument against sustainability governance instead derives from a broader rejection of state intervention. If market failures are denied, regulation is understood as coercion, and public institutions are portrayed as inefficient or captured by political interests, environmental intervention can be rejected without systematically contesting the underlying climate science. In this configuration, the central object of contestation shifts from whether climate change exists to whether the state has a legitimate role in addressing it.

The cultural dimension reinforces this anti-statist logic. Environmentalism is incorporated into a wider narrative linking socialism, "wokeism", feminism, reproductive rights and global governance. This resonates with research showing how environmental and climate politics can become embedded within broader ideological and cultural conflicts rather than remaining discrete policy disputes (reference: Forchtner / backlash references from 2.1–2.2). The Argentine case nevertheless adds a distinctive anti-statist component: the three forms of discursive delegitimization identified in our framework target the legitimacy of state intervention, the epistemic authority of public science and expertise, and the normative legitimacy of sustainability itself.

Crucially, these narratives do not remain confined to discourse. The principal targets of delegitimization closely correspond to the areas experiencing institutional erosion. State bureaucracies are portrayed as parasitic or captured while administrative structures and expenditure are reduced; scientists and universities are described as ideologically compromised while research institutions lose funding and personnel; and environmentalism is associated with a broader progressive agenda while environmental institutions are downgraded and regulatory protections weakened. This correspondence does not establish that particular statements caused individual reforms. It does, however, demonstrate that discursive delegitimization and institutional erosion form coherent components of the same governing project. In this respect, the findings connect scholarship concerned with the ideological construction of environmental opposition to research emphasizing that state institutions themselves are politically constituted and selectively reorganized (Jessop, 2002).

This is the central contribution of the concept of anti-statist sustainability backlash. Backlash need not primarily take the form of societal opposition to climate policies or attempts to undermine climate science. It can also originate within government and target the institutional infrastructure through which sustainability objectives are pursued.

**6.2 Institutional erosion as a pathway of policy dismantling**

The findings also extend the policy-dismantling literature by showing how substantial retrenchment can occur without immediate legislative repeal. Research on policy dismantling has demonstrated that governments can reduce policy commitments through changes in policy density and intensity and that dismantling strategies are shaped by political opportunities and constraints (Bauer et al.; Bauer & Knill). The Argentine case shows the importance of extending this perspective from policy instruments to the capacities underlying their implementation. This is particularly visible because Milei initially governed without control of Congress. While formal legislative change faced political constraints, retrenchment proceeded through budget cuts and under-execution, organizational downgrading, reassignment of responsibilities, dissolution of funds and staffing reductions.

Several environmental laws, climate commitments and policy instruments consequently remained formally in force while the financial, administrative and epistemic capacities required for their implementation deteriorated. Looking exclusively at formal policy change would therefore underestimate the extent of dismantling. The Argentine case illustrates a pattern of formal permanence with material incapacitation: legal obligations remain while the state progressively loses the capacity to fulfil them. This complements accounts of gradual institutional change in which substantial transformation can occur through processes other than formal institutional replacement (Mahoney & Thelen, 2010; Streeck & Thelen, 2005).

The Glacier Protection Law illustrates how this process can evolve when political opportunities change. Early attempts to modify environmental legislation encountered congressional resistance, while administrative and budgetary erosion could proceed through other channels. Following the changed parliamentary configuration after the 2025 midterm elections, formal rollback became more feasible. The glacier reform therefore reveals a possible sequence from delegitimization, through capacity erosion, to formal policy dismantling. This should not be understood as an inevitable progression. Rather, consistent with the dismantling literature, governments may rely on different strategies depending on the institutional and political constraints they face (Bauer & Knill, xx).

The findings also reinforce the value of approaching environmental governance through state and policy capacity rather than formal policy outputs alone. As Wu, Ramesh and Howlett (2015) emphasize, effective policy depends on analytical, operational and political capacities distributed across individuals, organizations and systems. Sustainability governance similarly depends upon coordination, knowledge production and institutional resources that extend beyond individual policy instruments (Lemos & Agrawal, 2006; Jordan & Huitema, 2014). From this perspective, reductions in scientific personnel, administrative expertise, coordinating authority and organizational resources constitute substantive governance changes even where statutory mandates survive.

This also raises questions about the durability of capacity erosion. Reinstating a regulation or restoring a budget may be easier than rebuilding organizations, experienced bureaucracies, scientific communities and institutional memory. Assessing sustainability-policy resilience therefore requires looking beyond the survival of legislation to the institutional capacities that make implementation possible.

**6.3 Implications for Argentina and beyond**

The Argentine case demonstrates how rapidly sustainability governance can be transformed even when environmental policy is not the principal axis of political competition. Milei entered government with an explicitly anti-statist programme rather than primarily an anti-environmental one. Sustainability institutions nevertheless became particularly exposed because environmental regulation, public science and international environmental governance could readily be incorporated into the broader categories of bureaucracy, casta, socialism and "wokeism". In this respect, the case illustrates the selective character of state restructuring emphasized by Jessop (2002): anti-statism does not necessarily entail the uniform retreat of the state, but rather political choices over which capacities and institutions should be weakened, maintained or reinforced.

The political response has also been uneven. Resistance has been visible around universities and science and around particular environmental issues, including the Glacier Law. This cautions against interpreting Milei's discourse as socially hegemonic. At the same time, resistance to individual reforms has not yet produced an equally integrated political counter-narrative defending the role of state capacity, public expertise and regulation in sustainability governance. The distinction between mobilization against particular reforms and political contestation of the broader anti-statist narrative deserves greater attention in research on sustainability backlash.

The case also has international relevance. Milei's cultural-backlash framing is more prominent in international than domestic speeches, where environmentalism is incorporated into a wider conflict involving socialism, "wokeism", multilateralism and Western values. The implications of anti-statist sustainability backlash may therefore travel through political narratives and repertoires rather than through direct replication of Argentine policies. Argentina's retreat from active climate diplomacy further shows that domestic ideological change can affect multilateral environmental governance even without formal withdrawal from international agreements. Comparative research should examine whether similar combinations of anti-statism, cultural backlash and institutional erosion emerge elsewhere, and under which institutional conditions they translate into policy change.

**6.4 Limitations and research agenda**

Three limitations are particularly important. First, qualitative coding involves interpretive choices, especially where anti-state, anti-expert and cultural narratives overlap. Coding frequencies should therefore be treated as descriptive indicators of the prominence of narratives within the corpus rather than direct measures of their political effects. Second, a single-case study cannot establish how widespread the identified mechanisms are. Argentina provides an analytically revealing case of explicit anti-statism, but comparative research is needed to establish whether similar dynamics occur under other political and institutional configurations.

Third, the close correspondence between discourse and institutional change does not establish a deterministic causal relationship. Macroeconomic adjustment, administrative reform and sector-specific interests also contributed to the observed changes. Process tracing and interviews could establish more precisely how ideological narratives enter individual governmental decisions. Future research should also examine the other side of the process: which institutions resist backlash, which actors construct effective counter-narratives, and whether lost sustainability capacities can subsequently be reconstructed.

**6.5 Conclusion**

This article introduced the concept of anti-statist sustainability backlash to capture a form of political opposition that goes beyond contesting individual environmental policies or denying climate science. The Argentine case shows how sustainability governance can be challenged simultaneously at two levels: discursively, by undermining the legitimacy of state intervention, public expertise and sustainability itself; and institutionally, by weakening the financial, administrative, regulatory and knowledge capacities through which the state governs sustainability. By bringing the sustainability-backlash literature into dialogue with scholarship on policy dismantling and state capacity, the article shows how ideological opposition can become translated into institutional transformation.

The broader implication is that sustainability backlash should be assessed not only through visible policy reversals but also through changes in the capacity of the state to act. Argentina illustrates how substantial dismantling can occur while laws and international commitments formally remain in place, producing formal permanence with material incapacitation. Understanding contemporary sustainability backlash therefore requires asking not only which policies governments reverse, but which institutions, expertise and capacities remain available to govern sustainability afterwards.
